translations.text: Teaching of our holy father Basil, which he delivered in the city of Lacizi.
Our enemy strives to drown out our word with his own uproar, but let us not be ignorant of his devices,
but let us turn our ears and our minds to those good and divine teachings, and let us have pity on those who do not listen to them.
And let us not wander in mind among vain things, but wherever we are in body, let us be there in mind as well.
Remember, then, those profitable words from the Scriptures that have been spoken since dawn.
Remember the teachings of the Psalms, the words of the Proverbs, the deeds in the lives of the saints, the apostolic commandments, and, before all else,
the majesty of the words of the Gospel, so that from all of this you may gather your profit and so depart in this way to your own [?].
For in this great church, just as there is diversity of faces, so too there is diversity of minds, and just as there is diversity of ages, so too there is diversity of sins.
For many are the snares of the devil, and he fights one person in one way and another in another:
toward whichever passion he sees the mind inclined, in that direction he wages the greater battle.
Now if anyone here is wounded in soul by envy, or pride, or anger - may there not be even one, by the power of the Lord, whom I implore for this.
But since it is difficult in human nature not to have some one of the passions,
small or great, for this reason I speak, so that each may receive the medicine for whatever sickness he has:
if you are envious, receive healing; if you are wrathful, the medicine is likewise ready,
for the holy Scriptures speak about all of this, and if we are able, let us also recite the words spoken by the saints about these things.
Again, if you are greedy, here is healing; if you are proud, here you may calm your pride and that swelling of the soul,
if only you are willing to drink, as from a richly gushing spring, those words of the saints and from the spiritual books, and so be healed.
First, then, hear the word of the Proverbs, which says:
"Whoever looks straight will be shown mercy," which teaches prudence of mind by means of its obscurity.
For do you understand why it says: "Whoever looks straight will be shown mercy"?
For it is voluntary acts that become praiseworthy or punishable, but looking straight does not come from our will; rather, it depends on what the thing seen is like.
For if we look at something crooked and contrived, how could we see it straight? For straight is that whose appearance is smooth and simple and not of many forms.
Since, then, the things of this world are disordered and not straight, how does Scripture praise the one who looks straight and condemn
the one who looks at mountains [?] and rocks and ravines, or a stormy sea, or anything else of this kind?
And would one who looks at such things be punished? And where is the justice of God, if anyone is punished for involuntary things?
But hear these words and understand what it is to look with an upright eye. For behold, two brothers are brought before you:
one poor and one rich, one a stranger and the other your own, either as litigants before you, if you are a judge, or to ask for something.
But you, if you sit as judge, do not look insincerely but uprightly, and do not acquit the rich man because of his wealth, if he is unjust.
Again, if two are brought before your door and ask you for something, do not look in a disorderly way and say, 'This one is mine and that one is a stranger.'
If you look in such a disorderly way, you will not receive mercy.
Look uprightly, for the nature of both is one: this one is a human being and that one too, and the need of both is equal.
Give to your brother, and give also to the stranger. Do not turn your brother away, and count the stranger too as your brother.
Do not honor your friend more than the stranger, for it is not partiality that has been commanded of you, but mercy.
It was not commanded that you should give to your own and not to the stranger. Or are we not all brothers to one another, since we are all children of one father?
If you are seeking the spiritual sense, there is one Father of all: God.
Again, if you speak of what is earthly, there is one mother of all: the earth, and we have all been made from one soil.
So now it is clear that we are brothers by nature, in the flesh, and we are brothers by that spiritual birth.
That poor man too has the same blood from the first man as you do, and he has received the same grace from God as you have.
Look uprightly, then, so that you may receive mercy. Do not say that this one is rich [?] and worthy of honor, and again that that one is poor and contemptible.
Do not be such a disorderly observer, for many times the rich man is a liar, the rich man is a robber, and the poor man is righteous.
But you, do not look at the face; go inside, make the distinction there, and give honor to the one who has what is honorable.
For what is honorable: virtue or wealth? Why do you examine the outward and give no thought to the hidden?
For if you see a rich man drowned in passions, understand that outwardly he has brass and inwardly clay.
Again, if you see a poor man adorned with virtue, he has earthenware outwardly and gold inwardly, and he is a treasure hidden in earthen vessels.
If this man is pure and the rich man a fornicator, who is truly rich?
The one who keeps purity, or the one who is in fornication and has grown rich by plunder?
For the wealth of the one endures forever, but that of the other lasts a little while. No thief steals the former's wealth, while the latter's is here today and gone tomorrow.
Understand all this in this way, so that you may look uprightly and receive mercy.
Again, if you are a lover of glory, you do not look uprightly; if you are wrathful, the same holds.
Understand everything in this way, so that you may find healing of the passions. Listen well to the Scriptures.
When you are prone to anger, say: Where is the cure for my passion? When you hear something about it, say: This is my concern, for I recognize my illness.
If you go to a house of healing and see the multitude of cures written in those many books, seek out what cure you may find for that illness of yours.
For it is not the one whose foot hurts who seeks medicine for the eye, but the one whose eye is burning who seeks a cure for the eye.
Now therefore let each one take from the Scriptures the medicine for his own passion.
If you are wrathful, dispel your wrath, for "a wrathful man is very ugly."
Learn from Scripture the loathsomeness of that ugly anger, since by yourself you are unable to see its ugliness,
what kind of sin anger is, and how ugly is the one who practices it: for he strips off the form of a man and puts on the form of a beast. His blood boils,
his eyes turn to fire; you see that the boiling blood seethes upon the heart, and his face becomes the color of blood.
If you see this, understand that ugliness. If he gnashes his teeth, understand that he resembles a boar whetting its teeth.
When that enraged man strikes out, he does not recognize his father and does not recognize his son because of that evil.
This is an evil ugliness. Beware of it, and if you see it in another, guard yourself all the more, for "a wrathful man is ugly."
And "do not associate with a wrathful man," so that you too may not become like him.
For he will say some insulting word to you and provoke you as well, and when you cannot bear it,
then you say something more evil to him, and he in turn says something worse to you, and thus you begin to shoot at one another with abuse, as with arrows.
He speaks a word of abuse; you do not bear it and say something worse; again he becomes inflamed all the more; and then whichever of you is given the victory is the more pitiable.
And for this reason I say: Do not keep company with an angry man,
"nor sit with an envious man." Envy is another evil passion, sown among people by the devil, and it eats away the heart as rust eats iron.
Envy is a passion that contains many evils. But one useful thing comes with it: its evil turns back on the very person who acts on it.
For the envious man is often unable to do any harm at all to the one he envies, but only eats away at himself with grief.

Again, hear this commandment too: "Do not move the boundary of the fathers" and "do not encroach upon the property of orphans," so that in this way you may enter that inheritance of yours, which is [?] the kingdom of heaven.
Do not seize your neighbor's land; do not add field to your fields.
For the more you multiply fields by injustice, the more you increase your sins, for "that land remains here" and after you it will belong to your heirs.
And that sin of yours will remain forever and will follow your soul as a shadow follows the body.
Do not therefore multiply your sins, for the illness of avarice has no end, but is like the nature of fire,
which, when it finds fuel, flares up all the more and does not stop until the fuel runs out.
Greed is likewise, for nothing is able to restrain it; it is worse than fire, and it seizes everything.

He takes the land of one neighbor; then another neighbor appears, and he seizes that one's too. He does not count up what he has acquired, but looks at what he has not acquired, asking why he does not have everything.
He does not rejoice over what he has, but mourns over what he does not have.
Then from this business unceasing anxiety comes upon him, and vain sleepless nights, and the more that wealth increases, the more his anxieties multiply.
He expects the coming of the judge and is afraid that at the tribunal the orphans whose property he seized may show him their tears and whimper.
For this reason he seeks out wicked false witnesses, so that in this way he may go to law and seize the ancestral land of that infant orphan.
Such anxieties as these consume his soul. He is suspicious of everyone and afraid of everyone:
he is afraid of his slaves, and he does not want to raise children, for fear that he might have to divide his property.
And some of his wealth he buries and some he wickedly squanders, yet he places his hope in what is buried.
That hope of his is a lost one, for if it were a matter of true hope, that money would have been given to the poor, so that he might have hope in heaven.
But he hides it in the ground, saying, "Perhaps it may be of use to me someday." But that use is unknown,
as to when that time may come; yet this is known, that the time will come when he will repent of his wicked designs.
So hear now these words of mine, which I speak concerning all the passions, so that each of you may strip off sin
like the old skin of a snake, and thus, made radiant, you may depart to your own homes.
For this is why this assembly exists, and this is why the fathers devised these gatherings: so that you may learn here the good will of God,
and flee sin and seek righteousness and not seize the property of orphans and widows.
Do not use your children as an excuse, saying, "It is for them that I toil." For if you have children, give them not sin but righteousness.
Leave to your children the memory of your good deeds rather than great wealth.
Make everyone a father to that child of yours, for the time of death and of departure from this world is going to come upon you, and that child of yours will be left behind.
Then, if you have been good and kind, everyone will raise that child of yours as their own, for they will remember that you too became a father to orphans.
But if your days have passed in wickedness and you have distressed everyone, and you have departed from here in that state, then from that moment you have left that child of yours an enemy to all,
for whoever sees him will be afraid, as of the young of a scorpion [?], that he may grow up and come to resemble his father's wickedness.
Now then, why do you gather many enemies for that child of yours?
For even if you were to live forever and death were not going to come, it would still be all the more your duty to make everyone your friend.
Since, then, the time of your death is unknown, hasten to leave behind many helpers for your child,
Or those of your children: perhaps you will die, and that plunder will not remain with them.
All this I tell you on the basis of human affairs; but as for what is the Lord's, you yourself know what the Gospel says to you.
For why do you make your son the excuse for your evil?
For he who created you also created him; and as he made you rich, he will make him rich too.
Do you not know that each person must give an account for his own life?
What do you know of whom you are storing up treasure for? For it is written: "They store up treasure and do not know who will gather it."
For many times a son is the excuse for that acquisition, but it becomes the inheritance of a robber or of a slanderer, or is carried off by plundering warriors.
Or tell me this: when you asked God for children, did you speak like this:
"Give me a son, so that I may become greedy and, on account of my children, be handed over to Gehenna? Give me children, so that I may not keep a single one of your commandments?"
No, you did not ask him in this way; rather, you asked for children who would be partakers of good, so that you might teach them virtue.
Now therefore do this: instruct them in what is good, and teach them to please God.
This is good wealth, if you leave this to your children: "Do not, then, encroach on the property of orphans."
"Nor sit down with an envious man," for envy is the work of the devil.
For the devil was not created a devil from the start; he had angelic authority, and he turned away from that nature and became a devil
through his own wickedness. So then, when he had fallen away from God and become estranged from his own proper state,
he saw man, how he was a living creature so small and yet more honored than all created things.
For he was older than man, and he saw that all living creatures had been created by the word of him who said:
"Let the waters bring forth creeping things with living souls," and by his word he created those great sea monsters that dwell in the impassable sea,
and by a word he created all the beasts: the great bulk of elephants and camels and horses and cattle; all of them were created in this way.
And heaven itself and the sun and moon and stars all came into being by a word, as did grasses and trees and the natures of the waters, those above and those of the earth.
But man alone was created by the hand of God. Then the devil saw that honor of man and rose up against him in envy, when he saw
how he was more honored than the sun; for the sun was created by command, but man by the hand; the sun was created for man's sake, but man for God's sake.
For man was created so that God might be glorified, but the sun so that it might serve men. In this way he considered that honor given to man.
He saw how all things were created and man only at the very last; like a king into an adorned palace, just so did man enter this world.
For he did not create man first, so that he would not be in want; rather, he first made heaven as a roof for him,
He established the earth firmly as a bearer of man, and made it adorned with every adornment of grasses and flowers, and all the beasts were given over to serve him.
And so the whole world awaited the one who was to dwell in all of it; then man was created.
God's love for humankind was not content that man should be on the earth only, but he also planted paradise and brought there his man, made with wisdom.
Then, when the devil saw such great honor spread upon man, with angels as his teachers and God himself speaking to him,
while that newly made living being was being instructed in every way so that he might come to the likeness of God, and when he saw this condition of his,
how by virtue he was attaining equality with the angels, yet as long as the man was alone, the devil had no means of harming him.
Then the woman was created as a weak living being, for God did well in making her nature soft, so that in this way she might nurture infants with mercy.
But when the devil saw her soft nature, he turned that readiness of hers, which she had for the virtues, toward evil.
This, then, is the devil's own passion: envy. Envy, whose evils no one can tell, which admits no healing.
For those who have a disease of the body tell the physician their disease, but what will the envious man say?
Or will he say, "My neighbor's good things distress me"? For this is the truth, but he is ashamed to say it.
For we calm dogs by petting them, but if someone does good to an envious man, he grows all the fiercer, for he does not rejoice
that good has been done to him, but is grieved because the other has the joy of being able to be his benefactor.
Do not, then, fall into that snare of the devil: he envied you, he envied you and drove you out of paradise.
Because of him thorns sprang up for you, because of him you eat bread in sweat, because of him you came to this land of exile.
But let that first fatherland of yours be in your memory; remember that former honor, remember that dwelling from which you were driven out, remember the one who deprived you of so many good things.
Never come to terms with him, never accept his talk, for he has done you two evils: first, that he cast you out from there, and second, that he prevents you from returning there.

He envied you at first and deceived you through a woman, and again he has found a means, so that through a woman once more he may not let you return there, for he devised fornication, so that in this way you cannot enter paradise.
That first injury, by which he brought you down, was not enough for him, but he seeks further means of halting your course.
And his devices are many, for his evils too are countless: rage, hatred, greed.
Everything that the word of truth abhors is all of the devil. He is a hater of humankind, for he is a fighter against God.
Since he became shameless toward God, he disregarded the Lord and became estranged from him.
Then he saw man, made in his image and likeness, and he was unable to fight against God;
therefore he emptied out his wickedness upon the image of God, like an angry man, enraged against a king,
he smashes his image, since he is unable to harm him; for this reason he strikes the wood on which his likeness is.
I have seen man-hating beasts, leopards, which by nature have rage against man.
And those who were provoking them drew the image of a man on paper and threw it to them.
But the beast, out of its great rage, does not discern what it is, but seizes it as if it were a man and tears the paper apart, and in this way it displays its hatred of man.
In the same way the devil displayed his hatred of God upon that image, since he had no power to touch God.
And so his warfare against us is a sign of his fighting against God and of his wickedness.
He brought the man down from Jerusalem to Jericho, from the height to the lowland, for Jerusalem is on a mountain, while Jericho is below, near the Salt Sea.
Whichever of you has seen that land knows that this statement is true, and that Jericho lies low in Palestine,
while Jerusalem is higher than all the surrounding places, on the mountain side.
And so the man came from the height to the lowland and went out from the stronghold of Jerusalem, to be handed over to those robbers of the desert, who wounded and stripped him.
First comes the wounding and then the stripping, for the wound of the soul is sin, and the stripping of the soul is being laid bare of the garment of incorruption.
And thus sin is what makes the grace vanish that was given to us through the washing of the second birth.
Fornication is a wound of the soul, and adultery in turn is another wound, and likewise envy: these are wounds of the soul,
which are inflicted by those robbers, the demons, who assist us in sin.
So after the wounding they stripped him of his garment, for if the matter had been a bodily one,
they would have stripped him first and wounded him afterward, so that the garment would not be damaged and he would be wounded all the more.
But as it is, first comes the wound and then the stripping, so that you may know that sin becomes the forerunner of your being laid bare of the grace
which the Lord gave you by his love for mankind; to him be glory and might, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
